claims.text: In Anthropic's Opus 4.5 comparison, a solo harness ran for 20 minutes and cost $9, while the full planner/generator/evaluator harness ran for 6 hours and cost $200, over 20 times more, with visibly better output.
On Anthropic's internal research evaluation, a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed a single Claude Opus 4 agent by 90.2%.
Anthropic's BrowseComp analysis found token usage alone explained 80% of performance variance, while token usage, tool-call count, and model choice together explained 95%.
Anthropic reports that ordinary agents typically use about 4x the tokens of chat interactions, while multi-agent systems use about 15x.

Anthropic recommends a two-stage harness for work spanning context windows: an initializer agent runs only in the first session to prepare the environment, and coding agents run in later sessions making incremental progress and leaving artifacts for the next session.
The initializer agent is instructed to create an init.sh setup script, a claude-progress.txt work log, and an initial Git commit showing what files were added.
The initializer expands the prompt into a comprehensive end-to-end feature list; Anthropic's Claude.ai-clone example had more than 200 features, initially marked failing.

Coding agents are told to edit the feature-list JSON only by changing a passes field and not to remove or rewrite tests; Anthropic found JSON less likely than Markdown to be inappropriately overwritten.

At the start of each session the coding agent inspects its working directory, reads progress notes, recent Git history and the feature list, starts the app via init.sh, runs a basic end-to-end smoke test, and picks the highest-priority unfinished feature; at the end it commits and writes a progress update.

Without explicit prompting, Claude sometimes marked features complete after code/unit tests or curl checks even when they failed end-to-end; browser automation improved detection, though Puppeteer MCP could not see browser-native alert modals.

Anthropic reports compaction alone was insufficient in the original long-running experiment: an Opus 4.5 loop could attempt too much, exhaust context mid-implementation leaving undocumented partial work, and later declare the project done prematurely.

Anthropic says Sonnet 4.5 showed context anxiety strongly enough that compaction alone was insufficient, while Opus 4.5 largely removed the behavior, allowing a continuous session with automatic compaction and no resets.

For models showing context anxiety, Anthropic recommends a clean context reset with a structured handoff; this prevents premature wrap-up but adds orchestration complexity, token overhead and latency.

The later full-stack harness used three agents: a planner expanding a 1-4 sentence prompt into a product spec, a generator implementing one feature at a time, and an evaluator using Playwright MCP against the live UI, API endpoints and database state.

Before each sprint, the generator and evaluator negotiated a file-based contract defining what done meant and how it would be verified; the evaluator failed the sprint if any criterion fell below a hard threshold.

Anthropic's Research system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern: a LeadResearcher plans, spawns parallel subagents, synthesizes findings, decides whether more research is needed, and passes results to a CitationAgent.

Anthropic says multi-agent systems fit breadth-first, parallelizable tasks exceeding one context window, while tasks requiring shared context or many dependencies, including many coding tasks, are poor fits today.
Each subagent delegation should specify an objective, output format, tool/source guidance and clear boundaries; vague instructions caused duplicated searches and gaps.
Anthropic's example effort budgets are one agent with 3-10 tool calls for simple fact-finding, 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each for comparisons, and more than 10 subagents for complex research.
Launching 3-5 subagents in parallel with subagents calling 3 or more tools in parallel reduced research time by up to 90%.
Early Research agents sometimes spawned 50 subagents for simple questions, searched endlessly for nonexistent sources, and over-relied on SEO content farms until source-quality prompting was added.

Anthropic recommends durable execution, resume-from-failure, retries, regular checkpoints, production tracing and artifact handoffs; synchronous subagent execution simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks.

The Claude Agent SDK is a Python/TypeScript library that runs the Claude Code binary, providing the same agent loop and context management, including built-in tools, hooks, subagents, MCP, permissions, sessions, Skills, memory and plugins.

An Agent Skill is a directory centered on SKILL.md; Claude loads the name and description first, reads the full SKILL.md only when relevant, then discovers deeper files or runs bundled code (progressive disclosure).

In the Messages API, Skills run in the code-execution container, up to 20 can be supplied per request, each version is a complete snapshot, and production integrations should pin a specific version rather than latest.
